bib.title: Chapter 3. Statistical Experiments and Significance Testing (Practical Statistics for Data Scientists, per source folder name)
bib.venue: book chapter (O'Reilly, per repo folder; publisher not printed in the extracted text)

question: How should data scientists design experiments (A/B tests) and judge whether an observed difference exceeds chance, and which classical inference tools matter in practice?

results.claim: Price A converted 200 of 23,739 and price B 182 of 22,588 page views; the 2x2 table is the chapter's running A/B example.
results.setup: Ecommerce price test, Table 3-2: price A 200 conversions / 23,539 none, price B 182 / 22,406.
results.quote: Price A converts almost 5% better than price B (0.8425% versus 0.8057%
results.note: Observed difference printed as 0.0368 percentage points and as 0.0368% in the permutation section.

results.claim: A permutation test (1,000 resamples) on the price test gives p = 0.308, so the 5% difference is within chance variation.
results.setup: Pooled urn of 382 ones and 45,945 zeros; one-sided (proportion of permuted differences exceeding observed).
results.quote:
The p-value is 0.308, which means that we would expect to achieve the same
result by random chance over 30% of the time.

results.claim: The normal approximation (prop.test, one-sided) on the same data gives p = 0.3498, close to the permutation p-value.
results.setup: 2-sample test for equality of proportions with continuity correction, alternative greater.
results.quote:
The normal approximation yields a p-value of 0.3498, which
is close to the p-value obtained from the permutation test.

results.claim: Web stickiness: page B's mean session time exceeded page A's by 21.4 seconds, but a permutation test says this is within chance variation.
results.n: 36 sessions: 21 for page A, 15 for page B; R = 1,000 permutations
results.setup: Proxy metric (time on interior page) from Google Analytics; last-session zeros removed.
results.quote: Page B has session times greater, on average, by 21.4 seconds versus page A.

results.claim: Welch t-test on the stickiness data gives p = 0.1408 (one-sided), near the permutation p-value of 0.124.
With 20 independent tests at alpha 0.05, the chance of at least one false positive is 0.64.
results.setup: 20 random predictors, one random outcome, alpha = 0.05, independence assumed (multiplication rule).
results.quote:
The probability
that at least one predictor will (falsely) test significant is the flip side of this
probability, or 1 – (probability that all will be nonsignificant) = 0.64.

results.claim: Bayer could fully replicate only 14 of 67 scientific studies it tried to replicate.
results.source: Bayer, 2011, as described in the chapter (no citation given)
results.setup: Cited as evidence that multiplicity makes more research not necessarily better.
results.quote:
when it tried to replicate 67
scientific studies, it could fully replicate only 14 of them.

results.claim: One-way ANOVA on four pages (5 visitors each): permutation p = 0.09278 versus F-test p = 0.0776 (F = 2.74).
results.setup: aovp (lmPerm) permutation ANOVA versus aov F-test on Table 3-3 stickiness data.
results.quote: The p-value, given by Pr(Prob), is 0.09278.

results.claim: Three headlines (1,000 visitors each) have chi-square statistic 1.666; resampled p = 0.4853, chi-square-distribution p = 0.4348, Fisher exact p = 0.4824.
results.n: clicks 14, 8, 12 of 1,000 each; 2000 simulation replicates; df = 2
results.setup: Table 3-4 click data; null of a shared 34/3,000 click rate.
results.note: Statistic printed as 1.666 in prose and 1.6659 in output; Fisher p-value 0.4824, chi-square distribution p-value 0.4348.

results.claim: Interior digits of 315 laboratory measurements departed from the uniform expectation of 31.5 per digit by far more than chance (chi-square test).
results.metric: expected count per digit under uniformity
results.setup: Imanishi-Kari case; Table 3-7 digit frequencies (e.g. digit 1: 71, digit 2: 7).
results.quote: The distribution of the 315 digits, shown in Figure 3-8 certainly looks nonrandom
results.note: The chi-square statistic and p-value are not printed.

results.claim: Power illustration: with a 1.1% baseline click rate and a 10% lift to 1.21%, 300 draws per group are far too few; even a 50% lift needs several thousand impressions.
results.metric: first-draw clicks, box A vs box B (n = 2,000)
results.setup: Simulated boxes at 1.1% and 1.65% click rate; a single draw, power not computed.
results.note: Prose says 'require a larger improvement (30% instead of 10%)' but then uses a 50% boost to 1.65%; the chapter's own inconsistency. First n = 300 draw gave 3 vs 5 ones.

results.claim: Revenue per page view has misleading SDs because most values are zero; mean absolute deviation (7.68 for A, 8.15 for B) is more reasonable.
results.unit: currency per page view (unit not stated)
results.setup: Price test of Table 3-1; means 3.87 (A) and 4.11 (B).
results.quote:
the mean absolute deviation from
the mean (7.68 for A and 8.15 for B) is more reasonable than the standard deviation.

results.claim: Bandit example: after 50 pulls per arm, arm A won 10, arm B 2, arm C 4.

limits: Chapter text does not print book authors, year or publisher; bib fields are unknown.
Examples are hypothetical or simplified single runs; no power curves or repeated-experiment results are shown.
The authors say formal tests matter little for data science and the p-value should not control decisions: 'a p-value should not be considered controlling'.
The Bonferroni description says it divides alpha by 'the number of observations n', where it should be the number of tests; flag this wording.
The chapter advises against rules of thumb such as 'wait for 1,000 visitors and run a week' but gives no general sample-size rule.
R code is shown; bandit algorithms and Thompson sampling are described only in outline, with no regret or simulation results.
practices: Decide the single test statistic or metric before running the experiment; choosing it afterwards invites researcher bias (A/B Testing).
Randomize subjects to treatments and include a control group so that differences are due to treatment or chance only (A/B Testing).
Use a permutation (resampling) test as a general-purpose, assumption-light check on whether a difference is within chance variation (Permutation Test).
Specify alpha before the test; treat a p-value as one input to a decision, not the controlling one (Statistical Significance and P-Values).
Interpret a p-value as the probability of results this extreme given a chance model, not the probability the result is due to chance (P-values, ASA principles).
Use a one-tail test when the default is kept unless the new option proves better; note software defaults to two-tail (One-Way, Two-Way Hypothesis Test).
Judge sample size by the number of rare events (conversions), not total rows, when rates are under 1% (Statistical Significance and P-Values).
For several groups, run one omnibus test (ANOVA) rather than many pairwise comparisons (ANOVA).
In predictive modelling guard against multiplicity with cross-validation and a holdout sample; otherwise use resampling benchmarks (Multiple Testing).
Use Fisher's exact test or resampling instead of the chi-square approximation when counts are very low (single digits) (Fisher's Exact Test).
Estimate power and sample size by simulating bootstrap samples with the target effect size, or with software specifying any three of sample size, effect size, alpha and power (Power and Sample Size).
Prefer multi-arm bandits when the goal is to find the best of several treatments rather than to establish significance (Multi-Arm Bandit Algorithm).
Check web-test visitors for systematic differences (time, device, season) as potential bias since random sampling cannot be fully implemented (ANOVA).

terms.definition: A group of subjects exposed to no (or standard) treatment.
The process of randomly assigning subjects to treatments.
The metric used to measure the effect of the treatment.
The hypothesis that chance is to blame.
Counterpoint to the null (what you hope to prove).
Hypothesis test that counts chance results only in one direction.
Hypothesis test that counts chance results in two directions.
The procedure of combining two or more samples together, and randomly (or exhaustively) reallocating the observations to resamples.
Given a chance model that embodies the null hypothesis, the p-value is the probability of obtaining results as unusual or extreme as the observed results.
The probability threshold of "unusualness" that chance results must surpass, for actual outcomes to be deemed statistically significant.
Mistakenly concluding an effect is real (when it is due to chance).
Mistakenly concluding an effect is due to chance (when it is real).
A standardized version of the test statistic.
Across multiple tests, the rate of making a Type 1 error.
The number of values free to vary in a statistic calculated from sample data.
A single hypothesis test of the overall variance among multiple group means.
A standardized statistic that measures the extent to which differences among group means exceeds what might be expected in a chance model.
A measure of the extent to which some observed data departs from expectation; the sum of squared Pearson residuals.
An imaginary slot machine with multiple arms for the customer to choose from, each with different payoffs, here taken to be an analogy for a multitreatment experiment.
The minimum size of the effect that you hope to be able to detect in a statistical test, such as "a 20% improvement in click rates".
The probability of detecting a given effect size with a given sample size.
With probability epsilon show A or B by a fair coin; otherwise show the offer with the highest response rate to date. Epsilon 1 is a plain A/B test, epsilon 0 is purely greedy.
